extracted.intended_audience: prospective beta readers and authors coordinating beta reads
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for people serving as beta readers (and for authors engaging them) about roles, timing, deliverables, format, expectations, payment, and when to accept or decline a beta-reading request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target-audience beta reader role
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers from your target audience whose main job is to share what they liked, what’s not working for them, and whether they’d buy the author’s book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These readers can be asked for specific feedback on issues like world building or character development but aren’t editors and aren’t expected to perform editing tasks. Some are paid, but most are not. They typically work with print copies or PDFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity readers and subject-matter experts role
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled readers (sensitivity readers and SMEs) hired to give targeted feedback on aspects such as portrayal of BIPOC/LGBTQIA+ characters or technical accuracy (e.g., quantum physics, surgical procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These readers are always paid for their work. It’s best to engage them just prior to querying or publishing — after drafting, revising, and proofreading — so the manuscript has gone through full development before their specific review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing-friend beta reader role
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers from critique groups, classes, conferences, or online communities (often other writers) who read for each other, usually at no cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best writing-friend readers are people who’ve never read the author’s work before. They often read manuscripts at various stages; their feedback is usually more substantial than a target-audience reader’s but less solution-focused than a professional editor’s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best timing/readiness for beta reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The best time to serve as a beta reader is after several drafts have been completed — one to get words on the page, one or two to shape the story, and a few additional ones to address pacing, timing, or character development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beta readers’ feedback is most useful when the work is relatively polished; sensitivity readers/SMEs should be engaged even later. Great beta readers have fresh eyes and typically read a manuscript only once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set expectations / have an honest conversation before agreeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting, ask for a one-page synopsis, the author’s deadline for feedback, how many drafts they’ve completed, and what developmental work they’ve done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the deadline or premise doesn’t work, or their answers suggest the work isn’t ready, respectfully decline or ask to read later. Spell out what 'ready' means for your role so the author knows when to contact you. It’s okay to go back and have this conversation even after initially agreeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission format and preconditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree on the format and presentation of the manuscript before reading: submission date, file format (print/PDF for target readers; MS Word/Pages/Google Docs for writing friends and sensitivity readers who need to comment), and document formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the document to be double spaced, paginated, include numbered chapters, and have the author’s name and title in the header. Request that a comprehensive spell check and a read-aloud pass have been completed prior to submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-chapter trial period
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a first-chapter 'trial period' so the reader and author can test fit before committing to the whole manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trial lets the reader bow out early if the work doesn’t resonate, protecting the reader’s time and giving the author clear feedback about fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and specificity of feedback (ask focused questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors will often ask beta readers several specific questions (e.g., about character development); focused readings should have questions known in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general readings, authors may provide questions later so they don’t color the reader’s first impressions. Clarify whether the read is a focused diagnostic or a general impression to avoid mismatched expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to stop or decline mid-process
rubrics_metrics.description: If guidelines aren’t followed, the manuscript isn’t ready, or the work doesn’t speak to you, it’s acceptable to stop reading and inform the author you’re not the right reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although it may feel awkward, stopping benefits both parties: the writer learns problems exist and can address them or find a better match; you preserve enthusiasm for future collaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags that indicate a manuscript isn’t ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Two specific red flags are a new writer who hasn’t taken any classes and a manuscript that is a first draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these red flags appear when you ask about the project, suggest the author do more developmental work before you commit to reading — offer to read later after revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment norms and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment expectations vary by role: sensitivity readers and subject-matter experts are always paid; some target-audience readers are paid but most are not; writing friends often perform the task for free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify payment up front when engaging readers who perform professional or specialized work, and set expectations for compensation appropriate to the reader’s role and the depth of feedback requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve fresh-eye value (read once)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable trait of great beta readers is having fresh eyes and generally reading a manuscript only once to provide first-impression feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rewinding and re-reading sections multiple times unless previously agreed; the one-pass perspective is useful to authors assessing overall resonance and major issues.
